title: Ramakrishna and tantra's reputation
hookLine: a saint walks the whole tantric path, and the wine never reaches his lips
carry: the offering makes the rite, not the substance
tomorrow: who decides the order of a temple's whole day?

lines: A WOMAN TEACHER OF THE TANTRAS.
cards: Calcutta, the eighteen-sixties. In the temple garden at Dakshineswar lives a priest of the goddess Kali named Ramakrishna.

One day a wandering woman teacher arrives, known as the Bhairavi Brahmani, deeply learned in the Tantras. For about two years, by his disciples' accounts, she leads him through one tantric discipline after another.
Some of those rites use things the usual rules of worship keep out, wine among them. So what happens when the cup comes to the priest?

teach.h: HE TOUCHED IT TO HIS FOREHEAD.
teach.b: The accounts say he couldn't drink it. He touched a drop to his forehead, already lost in the Mother, and that was all. Through every rite he saw each woman as the Mother herself.
That's the true shape of tantra's reputation. Some rites, in some lineages, really did offer things the ordinary purity rules forbid, wine and meat among them.
The idea was bold: if everything is the goddess's power, nothing is outside her, not even what the usual rules call unclean. But the Tantras guard their own door.
The Kularnava Tantra says, in effect: if drinking wine brought perfection, every drunkard would be perfect; if eating meat did, every meat-eater would be holy.
Done for appetite, the rite is no path at all. Here's the teaching. In tantra the substance isn't the rite.
The offering is: knowing who it's for. Lineages answer this differently, and none is ranked here.
Some call themselves the right-hand way, dakshina, and keep worship inside the familiar rules.
Others follow the left-hand way, vama, where such rites belong, under a teacher and strict conditions. Many use substitutes, milk or fruit.
So the rumor holds one true thread, cut loose from everything that held it in place.

how: Tantric lineages differ: some keep to conventional worship, some perform rites with normally forbidden substances under a teacher, and some use substitutes or read them symbolically.

games.q: what does “what tantra actually is” mean?
o: a path whose rites are mainly about wine and feasting
a path that permits anything done in the goddess's name
a path whose own books warn appetite is no path

games.q: the reputation, met head on. tap the pairs.
p: touched the wine only to his forehead

s: tantra is mostly about wine and breaking rules
one thread is real, in some lineages, under a teacher and strict conditions; the books are mostly worship.
a Tantra itself warns that wine alone makes no one perfect
the Kularnava: if it did, every drunkard would be perfect.
every tantric lineage uses wine and meat in worship
some call themselves the right-hand way and keep to familiar rules; some use substitutes.

games.q: a post going around says 'tantra means anything goes.' a friend asks what the Kularnava would say back. what's closest?
o: if wine alone made people perfect, every drunkard would be.
it agrees: the rites exist to give permission for pleasure.
nothing; the Tantras never mention forbidden things at all.
games.why: the Kularnava names the rites' danger itself: done for appetite, they're no path. some lineages kept such rites under strict conditions; others kept familiar rules or used symbols.

practice: Many Hindus offer food and water to the deity before taking any themselves; what comes back is prasad, blessed.
If there's water near you and you pray, offer it first in your mind, then take one sip and hold it: its coolness, its weight, the moment it goes down.
If you don't, simply take the sip with your whole attention, and stay with the aftertaste for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: What tantra actually is: here, a path whose own book says the substance isn't the rite, and appetite isn't a path.

orig.note: Sanskrit: left; vama, the left-hand way, names lineages whose rites cross the usual purity rules, under strict conditions.

carryVoice: Something to keep: the offering makes the rite, not the substance. Ramakrishna's cup showed it. See you tomorrow.
